title: Acids, Bases & pH
description: Properties of acids and alkalis, the pH scale, indicators, neutralisation reactions, making salts, and everyday uses of acids and bases.

notes.heading: The pH Scale and Indicators
notes.body: The pH scale (0-14) measures the acidity or alkalinity of a solution: pH 7 = neutral (pure water). pH below 7 = acidic (lower = stronger acid). pH above 7 = alkaline (higher = stronger alkali). The scale is logarithmic — each step of 1 represents a 10× change in H⁺ concentration. pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4, and 100× more acidic than pH 5. Indicators are substances that change colour depending on pH: Litmus — red in acid, blue in alkali. Universal indicator — a mixture of indicators giving a full spectrum: red (pH 0-3 strong acid), orange (4-5 weak acid), green (pH 7 neutral), blue (8-10 weak alkali), purple (11-14 strong alkali). Phenolphthalein — colourless in acid, pink in alkali (used in titrations). Methyl orange — red in acid, yellow in alkali. pH can be measured with universal indicator paper/solution, a pH meter (more precise), or data loggers. Natural indicators: red cabbage juice turns red in acid, green/blue in neutral, yellow in alkali.

illustration.alt: The pH scale from 0 to 14 with colour zones and indicator colour changes.
illustration.caption: The pH scale is logarithmic; universal indicator gives a full colour range from red (strong acid) to purple (strong alkali).

notes.heading: Acids: Properties and Examples
notes.body: An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water. Common laboratory acids: Hydrochloric acid (HCl), Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), Nitric acid (HNO₃). Common household acids: citric acid (lemons, oranges), ethanoic acid (vinegar), carbonic acid (fizzy drinks — CO₂ dissolved in water). Properties of acids: sour taste (do NOT taste lab acids!), corrosive (can burn skin and damage materials), turn litmus red, react with metals to produce hydrogen gas (metal + acid → salt + hydrogen), react with metal oxides/hydroxides (neutralisation), react with carbonates to produce CO₂ (acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide). Strong acids (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃) fully ionise in water — every molecule releases its H⁺. Weak acids (ethanoic, citric, carbonic) only partially ionise — most molecules keep their H⁺. This means a dilute solution of a strong acid may have a higher pH than a concentrated solution of a weak acid — concentration and strength are different concepts.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing strong and weak acid ionisation and the properties of acids.
illustration.caption: Strong acids fully ionise in water, while weak acids only partially ionise.

notes.heading: Bases and Alkalis
notes.body: A base is a substance that neutralises an acid to form a salt and water. Metal oxides (e.g., CuO, MgO) and metal hydroxides (e.g., NaOH, Ca(OH)₂) are bases. An ALKALI is a soluble base — it dissolves in water to release hydroxide ions (OH⁻). Common alkalis: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH — 'caustic soda'), Potassium hydroxide (KOH), Calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂ — 'lime water'), Ammonia solution (NH₃(aq)). Properties of alkalis: bitter taste (do NOT taste!), soapy feel, corrosive, turn litmus blue, neutralise acids. Strong alkalis (NaOH, KOH) fully ionise in water. Neutralisation occurs when H⁺ (from acid) reacts with OH⁻ (from alkali) to form water: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. This is the fundamental reaction of neutralisation. The other ions (from the acid's anion and the base's cation) form the salt. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Ionic equation: H⁺ + Cl⁻ + Na⁺ + OH⁻ → Na⁺ + Cl⁻ + H₂O. The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions (they don't change); the essential reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

illustration.alt: Diagram distinguishing bases and alkalis and showing neutralisation as H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
illustration.caption: Alkalis release OH⁻ ions in water; neutralisation forms water from H⁺ and OH⁻.

notes.heading: Making Salts
notes.body: A salt is an ionic compound formed when the H⁺ in an acid is replaced by a metal ion or ammonium ion. The name of the salt comes from the acid used: Hydrochloric acid → chloride salts (NaCl, KCl, CaCl₂). Sulfuric acid → sulfate salts (Na₂SO₄, CuSO₄, MgSO₄). Nitric acid → nitrate salts (KNO₃, NaNO₃, AgNO₃). Methods for making soluble salts: (1) Acid + insoluble base (metal oxide/hydroxide/carbonate) — add excess solid to acid, warm gently, filter off excess, evaporate filtrate to crystallisation point, leave to crystallise. Example: CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l). The blue solution yields blue CuSO₄·5H₂O crystals. (2) Acid + alkali (titration) — used when both reactants are soluble (no filtration possible). An indicator shows the exact neutralisation point. Repeat without indicator to get pure salt solution, then crystallise. (3) Acid + metal (for reactive metals like Mg, Zn, Fe) — metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Example: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑. Method for insoluble salts: precipitation — mix two soluble salts containing the required ions. The insoluble salt precipitates out. Filter, wash with distilled water, dry. Example: BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq).

illustration.alt: Methods for making soluble salts and precipitation for insoluble salts.
illustration.caption: The parent acid determines the salt name, and the method depends on whether the base is soluble.

notes.heading: Reactions of Acids (Summary)
notes.body: Acids undergo characteristic reactions: (1) Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen. Example: 2HCl + Mg → MgCl₂ + H₂↑. Test for H₂: lighted splint gives a 'squeaky pop'. NOT all metals react — only those above hydrogen in the reactivity series (Mg, Al, Zn, Fe). Copper and silver do NOT react with acids. (2) Acid + Metal oxide → Salt + Water. Example: H₂SO₄ + CuO → CuSO₄ + H₂O. (3) Acid + Metal hydroxide → Salt + Water. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. (4) Acid + Metal carbonate → Salt + Water + Carbon dioxide. Example: 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. Test for CO₂: bubble through limewater → turns milky/cloudy. (5) Acid + Metal hydrogencarbonate → Salt + Water + CO₂. Example: HCl + NaHCO₃ → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Important: the gas produced depends on what the acid reacts with. Metals → H₂. Carbonates → CO₂. Oxides/hydroxides → no gas, just salt + water.

illustration.alt: Summary cards of the five characteristic reactions of acids.
illustration.caption: Acids react with metals, oxides, hydroxides, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates, each giving a characteristic product set.

notes.heading: Everyday Acids, Bases and Neutralisation
notes.body: Neutralisation has many practical applications: (1) Agriculture — lime (calcium oxide, CaO, or calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂) is spread on acidic soil to raise pH. Most crops grow best at pH 6-7. (2) Medicine — antacid tablets (containing CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂, or Al(OH)₃) neutralise excess stomach acid (HCl), relieving indigestion and heartburn. Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. (3) Industry — acidic industrial waste is treated with slaked lime before release into rivers. Flue gas desulfurisation: SO₂ (from power stations, causes acid rain) is removed by reacting with CaO or CaCO₃. (4) Personal care — shampoo is slightly acidic (pH ~5.5) to match the scalp's natural pH; soap is alkaline. Bee stings are acidic (treated with baking soda — a base). Wasp stings are alkaline (treated with vinegar — an acid). (5) Food — baking powder contains NaHCO₃ (sodium hydrogencarbonate), which releases CO₂ when heated or mixed with acidic ingredients (like buttermilk), making cakes rise. Tooth decay: bacteria in the mouth produce acid from sugar, which dissolves tooth enamel. Fluoride toothpaste helps remineralise enamel and resist acid.

illustration.alt: Everyday examples of neutralisation in agriculture, medicine, industry, food and personal care.
illustration.caption: Neutralisation is used to treat acidic soil, stomach acid, industrial waste and insect stings.

notes.heading: pH Practical Skills and Titration
notes.body: Measuring pH accurately: (1) Use a clean glass rod to transfer a drop of solution to universal indicator paper — do NOT dip the paper into the test tube (contaminates the solution). (2) Compare the colour to the chart immediately. (3) A pH meter (probe connected to a data logger) gives precise numerical values. Titration is a technique to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a given volume of alkali (or vice versa). Steps: (1) Pipette a known volume of alkali into a conical flask. (2) Add a few drops of indicator (phenolphthalein — pink in alkali, colourless in acid). (3) Fill a burette with acid of known concentration. (4) Slowly add acid, swirling the flask constantly. (5) As the endpoint approaches, add drop by drop until the indicator just changes colour (pink → colourless). (6) Record the volume of acid used (titre). (7) Repeat to get concordant results (within 0.1 cm³). Use the titre to calculate the concentration of the unknown solution. Titration is a fundamental analytical technique used in quality control, water testing, and pharmaceutical manufacturing.

illustration.alt: Correct pH measurement technique and a labelled titration apparatus.
illustration.caption: Use a clean glass rod for indicator paper and add acid from a burette dropwise near the endpoint.

flashcards.definition: Scale 0-14 measuring acidity/alkalinity. pH 7 = neutral, <7 = acid, >7 = alkali. Logarithmic: each step = 10× change in H⁺ concentration.
flashcards.example: pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4, and 100× more acidic than pH 5.

flashcards.definition: A substance releasing H⁺ ions in water. pH < 7. Turns litmus red. Reacts with metals, bases, and carbonates.
flashcards.example: HCl (hydrochloric), H₂SO₄ (sulfuric), citric acid (lemons), ethanoic acid (vinegar).

flashcards.definition: A soluble base that releases OH⁻ ions in water. pH > 7. Turns litmus blue. Feels soapy.
flashcards.example: NaOH (sodium hydroxide/caustic soda), KOH, Ca(OH)₂ (lime water), NH₃ (ammonia).

flashcards.definition: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Acid + base → salt + water. The fundamental acid-base reaction.
flashcards.example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Ionic: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions.

flashcards.definition: An ionic compound formed when the H⁺ in an acid is replaced by a metal ion (or NH₄⁺). Named from the parent acid.
flashcards.example: HCl → chloride salts; H₂SO₄ → sulfate salts; HNO₃ → nitrate salts.

flashcards.definition: A mixture of indicators giving a full colour range across pH 0-14: red (strong acid) → orange/yellow → green (neutral) → blue → purple (strong alkali).
flashcards.example: Lemon juice (pH ~2) gives a red colour; baking soda solution (pH ~9) gives blue.

flashcards.definition: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas. Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react.
flashcards.example: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑. Test H₂: lighted splint → 'squeaky pop'.

flashcards.definition: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
flashcards.example: 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. Test CO₂: bubble through limewater → milky/cloudy.

flashcards.definition: An ion present in a reaction mixture that does NOT participate in the reaction — it remains unchanged in solution.
flashcards.example: In NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions. The reaction is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

flashcards.definition: A technique to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali (or vice versa) using a burette and indicator.
flashcards.example: Phenolphthalein turns from pink (alkali) to colourless (acid) at the endpoint.

flashcards.definition: Strong acid: fully ionises in water (every molecule releases H⁺). Weak acid: partially ionises. Concentration ≠ strength.
flashcards.example: HCl is strong (fully ionised). Ethanoic acid (vinegar) is weak. A concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a dilute strong acid.

flashcards.definition: A mild base (CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃) taken to neutralise excess stomach acid and relieve indigestion/heartburn.
flashcards.example: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. The antacid neutralises stomach HCl.

questions.explanation: pH 2 is far below 7 — strongly acidic. Compare: stomach acid is pH 1-3.

questions.stem: Litmus paper turns blue in which type of solution?
questions.explanation: Litmus is red in acid, blue in alkali. 'Blue base' is a useful memory aid.
Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

questions.stem: Soil pH 5. What should a farmer add?
choices: Lime (an alkali like CaO or Ca(OH)₂)
questions.explanation: Acidic soil needs an alkali to neutralise it and raise the pH towards neutral (~6.5-7), which most crops prefer.
2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The CO₂ turns limewater milky — this is the test for carbonates.

questions.stem: A solution has pH 6. Another has pH 4. How many times more acidic is pH 4?
questions.explanation: Each pH step = 10×. From pH 6 to pH 4 is 2 steps → 10 × 10 = 100× more acidic at pH 4.

questions.stem: Which gas is produced when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
choices: Hydrogen — test with a lighted splint for a 'squeaky pop'
questions.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑.

questions.stem: Why does copper NOT react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
choices: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series — it cannot displace H⁺ ions
questions.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series (Mg, Al, Zn, Fe) react with acids. Copper, silver, and gold are below hydrogen → no reaction.

questions.stem: In the reaction HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, which ions are spectator ions?
choices: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ — they remain unchanged in solution
No spectator ions — all ions react
questions.explanation: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are present before and after the reaction unchanged. The net ionic equation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

questions.stem: What salt is produced when sulfuric acid neutralises potassium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulfuric acid → sulfate salts.

questions.stem: A bee sting is acidic. Which household substance would neutralise it?
questions.explanation: Acid + alkali → neutralisation. Baking soda (NaHCO₃) is a mild alkali that neutralises the acidic bee venom. Wasp stings are alkaline — treated with vinegar.

questions.stem: In a titration, why is a conical flask preferred over a beaker?
choices: The narrow neck reduces splashing and the swirling motion mixes solutions effectively without spilling
It prevents the indicator from changing colour
questions.explanation: The conical shape allows vigorous swirling for mixing while the narrow neck minimises splashing. This ensures accurate mixing as the endpoint is approached.

questions.stem: Antacid tablets often contain calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). How do they work?
choices: They kill bacteria in the stomach
CaCO₃ neutralises excess HCl in the stomach: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
They absorb water in the stomach
questions.explanation: Antacids provide a mild base that neutralises stomach acid (HCl), raising pH and relieving the burning sensation of indigestion.

questions.stem: Which statement about strong and weak acids is correct?
choices: Strong acids are always more concentrated than weak acids
A strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid at the same concentration
All acids have the same pH
questions.explanation: HCl (strong) at 0.1 mol/dm³ has a lower pH (~1) than ethanoic acid (weak) at 0.1 mol/dm³ (~3), because HCl fully ionises, releasing more H⁺.

questions.stem: Baking powder contains NaHCO₃. Why does it make cakes rise?
choices: When heated or mixed with acidic ingredients, NaHCO₃ decomposes releasing CO₂ gas bubbles that expand in the hot batter
It reacts with oxygen to form a foam
questions.explanation: Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases CO₂ when heated (thermal decomposition) or when reacted with acid. The gas bubbles become trapped in the batter, causing it to rise.
